title: Same pipeline, same data, 5 variants each. One strategy holds up, one is junk, and a plain out-of-sample test passes both.
author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
selftext:
Following on from the year-long field report someone posted here last week. I want to add one piece with actual output attached instead of opinions.



Context: my co-founder wrote his Master's thesis in Mathematics and Finance at Imperial on a multi-agent pipeline where an LLM proposes factors and a deterministic harness scores them, with the rule that the model never influences its own reward. I build the product around it. Everything below is from one run, provenance stamped, and I will post the config for anyone who wants it.



Setup, identical for both: S&P 100, daily bars, 2020-01-01 to 2026-06-22, yfinance, LightGBM on top of LLM-proposed factors, 5 variants tried, CSCV with 70 splits.



Strategy A, volume-adjusted breakout

in-sample Sharpe 2.01

out-of-sample Sharpe 0.67

plain out-of-sample check: passes

probability of backtest overfitting: 74 percent

verdict: likely overfit, do not put money on it



Strategy B, mean-reversion and momentum

in-sample Sharpe 5.16

out-of-sample Sharpe 2.07

plain out-of-sample check: passes

probability of backtest overfitting: 0 percent

verdict: holds



The one to look at is A. It made money out of sample. A plain train/test split signs off on it. It is still junk, because across the variants tried, the in-sample and out-of-sample rankings came apart badly enough that the survivor is best explained by selection rather than by an edge. CSCV catches that. A single holdout structurally cannot, because a single holdout has no way of knowing how many other candidates you graded against it.



Second thing worth noticing: both strategies lose roughly two thirds of their Sharpe going from in-sample to out-of-sample. 67 percent for A, 60 percent for B. That is what an intact result looks like. If your backtest does not decay like that, the interesting question is not what you found, it is what leaked.



Now the parts you should attack, because I would.



Five trials is a small search. Deflation and PBO are only ever as good as the trial count you feed them, and that count has to include everything you killed. This is the weakest joint in every setup of this kind, ours included, and anyone showing you deflated numbers without telling you the denominator is showing you nothing.



An in-sample Sharpe of 5 is a warning sign, not a brag. I am posting it because it is what the run produced. Daily S&P 100 with a 5 bps cost assumption is a forgiving environment.



This is one run, on liquid US equities, on public data. It says nothing about futures, crypto or anything intraday.



What I want from this thread:



If you run automated search, do you keep a trial counter that persists across sessions and includes discards? Everyone I ask says it is a discipline thing, which means it is not a counter.



Has anyone found a defense against the selection ratchet better than CSCV plus counting properly? Something that prevents it rather than measuring it afterwards is what I keep looking for.



Blunt answers welcome, including "your Sharpe numbers mean you have a bug". If that is the answer I would rather hear it here than find out later.
